planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or fall into gritty, sharply drained, lean soil in full sun; this smaller, woody-based species stays lower and tighter than Iberis sempervirens and resents any standing moisture around its crown.

directions: Rock candytuft is a dwarf, woody-based subshrub distinct from the more common Iberis sempervirens, forming a low, spreading mound of narrow, dark evergreen leaves that hugs crevices and scree slopes. In early to mid-spring it produces dense, flattened clusters of small white four-petaled flowers that blanket the tight mound before the true foliage color reasserts itself for the rest of the season. Grow in gritty, sharply drained, lean soil in full sun; it is native to rocky Mediterranean mountain slopes and performs poorly in heavy or moisture-retentive soils, where crown rot quickly sets in. Its diminutive size makes it especially well suited to troughs, scree beds, and tight crevices between paving stones, where larger candytufts would overwhelm the space.

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; this trademarked selection (sold as Snowsurfer) is bred for a tighter, more floriferous mound than older candytuft cultivars.

directions: Marketed under the trade name Snowsurfer, this compact selection of evergreen candytuft forms a tight, mounded cushion of narrow dark-green leaves that is smothered each spring in bright white flower clusters, with a noticeably denser and more uniform habit than seed-grown candytuft. Grow in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; it tolerates light afternoon shade in hot climates but blooms most heavily with a full day of sun. Once established it is drought tolerant and handles poor, rocky soils well, making it dependable for edging, rock garden pockets, and small-space plantings where a tidier scale is wanted. Shear lightly after the spring flush to keep the mound dense and to encourage a possible light rebloom later in the season.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants after the last frost into gritty, lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this species is less cold-hardy than Iberis sempervirens and benefits from a sheltered site or winter protection at the cold edge of its range.

directions: Native to the rocky coasts of Gibraltar and Morocco, this larger, more shrubby candytuft produces bigger leaves and showier flower clusters than Iberis sempervirens, opening white and aging to a soft lilac-pink so that older and newer flowers create a two-toned effect on the same plant. Grow in gritty, lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; it is somewhat less cold-hardy than the common evergreen candytuft and appreciates a warm, sheltered position in colder parts of its range. It tolerates heat, drought, and coastal salt exposure once established, making it a good choice for Mediterranean-style gravel gardens and dry rock walls. Shear lightly after the main spring bloom to maintain a dense, rounded form and to encourage fresh growth.

planting.note: Sow in early spring or fall into lean, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; this heavy-blooming selection (also sold as 'Schneehaube') breeds true from seed and forms a denser mat than the straight species.

directions: 'Snowcap' is a heavy-flowering selection of Caucasus rock cress prized for producing an unusually dense, uniform carpet of pure white spring bloom over gray-green, felted foliage, outperforming typical seed-grown Arabis caucasica in flower coverage. Grow in lean, gritty, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; like other rock cress it declines quickly in rich or waterlogged ground. It tolerates poor, rocky soil and drought well once established and is a reliable choice for cascading over dry walls, filling rock garden pockets, or edging sunny paths. Shear back by half immediately after flowering to keep the mat tight and to encourage strong bloom the following spring.

common_name: Spring Charm Rock Cress (Coast Rock Cress)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or early spring into sandy, coarse-grained, fast-draining soil; this California coastal native prefers mild winters without hard freezes and resents summer irrigation once established.

directions: Native to coastal bluffs and outcrops of the San Francisco Bay Area, 'Spring Charm' forms a fast-growing, dense mat of deep-green foliage and is covered in late winter to early spring with masses of small, sweetly fragrant, carmine-rose flowers on wiry stems. Grow in sandy or gravelly, fast-draining, low-fertility soil; give it full sun in cool coastal gardens but light afternoon shade inland, where summer heat and dry air are more intense. It thrives on minimal summer water and tolerates wind and salt spray, but fails quickly in heavy clay or where irrigation continues through the dry season. Excellent trailing over low rock walls, tucked into crevices, or massed as a flowering edge in a low-water native planting.

planting.note: Sow or transplant into well-drained, alkaline, gritty soil in full sun; part of the trailing Cascade breeding series, selected for long stems and deep purple color rather than the tighter mound of older aubrieta strains.

directions: A color selection within the vigorous Cascade breeding series, 'Cascade Purple' produces a profusion of deep violet-purple, four-petaled flowers with small yellow eyes over soft gray-green foliage, with notably longer trailing stems than older, mound-forming aubrieta strains. Grow in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, gritty soil in full sun; it tolerates light shade but flowers less heavily there. Its cascading habit makes it especially effective spilling over retaining walls, raised beds, and the edges of containers rather than staying in a tight clump. Shear back by about half immediately after the main spring bloom to keep growth dense and to encourage a tidier summer habit and possible rebloom.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in very well-drained, lean, alkaline soil in full sun; this old, reliable selection is best increased by softwood cuttings or division to keep its rich violet-blue color true.

directions: One of the oldest named aubrieta selections still widely grown, 'Doctor Mules' forms a low, wide-spreading mat of small, soft green, slightly scurfy leaves and bears single, rich violet-blue flowers in a dense spring flush. Grow in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; it is an excellent choice for dry chalky slopes, gravel gardens, and the tops of dry stone walls, where its natural cascading habit can spill freely. It tolerates light shade but performs best in full sun, and struggles where summers are hot and humid. Shear the plant back hard right after flowering to prevent the center from thinning out and to keep the mat dense and floriferous for the following year.

planting.note: Plant nursery starts in spring into well-drained soil, including wall crevices and paving gaps, in full sun; this named selection is propagated vegetatively to keep its heavier bloom and habit true.

directions: 'Profusion' is a heavier-flowering selection of Mexican fleabane, forming wide, wiry mats of small gray-green leaves that produce an especially generous, near-continuous flush of small daisy flowers from late spring through autumn — opening white and fading through blush-pink to rose as they age, so a single plant carries several flower colors at once. Grow in well-drained soil, including thin soil in wall crevices and paving cracks, in full sun to light shade. It self-seeds readily in favorable sites in addition to spreading by rhizome, quickly softening the edges of steps, gravel paths, and retaining walls. Trim back hard in early spring to remove winter-worn growth and encourage a fresh, dense flush of new stems.

planting.note: Set out divisions or nursery starts in fall or early spring into well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; named for California native plant authority Wayne Roderick, this selection is propagated vegetatively to preserve its deep flower color.

directions: Named for celebrated California native plant authority Wayne Roderick, this selection of seaside daisy is prized for the darkest flower color of the group — deep lavender-purple to violet-blue petals surrounding a bright golden disc, held over low, tidy mounds of gray-green foliage. Grow in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; it tolerates sandy, low-fertility ground and handles salt spray, wind, and drought once established, making it well suited to coastal and dry-garden plantings. Bloom is heaviest in spring but continues sporadically into fall, especially if spent flower stems are removed. Its compact habit and long bloom season make it a strong choice along pathways, in rock gardens, or massed as a flowering groundcover.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants in spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; this German-bred selection (also listed as 'Azurfee') bears larger, semi-double flowers than the wild species.

directions: 'Azure Fairy' is a robust selection of showy fleabane bearing larger, semi-double, narrow-rayed lavender-blue daisies with golden centers on sturdy stems, giving a fuller, more refined flower than the wild species. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun; it adapts readily to typical garden conditions at lower elevations despite its Rocky Mountain montane origins. Plants bloom heavily over several weeks in early to midsummer and attract a wide range of bees and butterflies, with the sturdy stems holding up well without staking. Deadhead spent flowers to prolong bloom and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor.
